turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, give me a second, this computer is crawling. Right — what has you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the knee, doctor. The right one. Going down the stairs it's a pure terror, and it wakes me at night when I turn.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has the pain been there?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Well the stairs in the house are steep, you know, in Raheny. We never got the rail fixed after himself passed, and I go down sideways.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, I was reading the screen. How long has the knee pain itself been going on?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. Since around Christmas, I'd say. Four months, maybe a bit more.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Worse coming down than going up?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Down, yes. Up is grand. At night if I roll over it catches me fierce.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any swelling?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit puffy some evenings, not every day. My sister says I should be doing the exercises off the telly, but I haven't the patience for that fella on the morning programme.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): The screen jumped on me. Swelling some evenings — is that what you said?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, a bit, of an evening.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stiff in the morning?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): About twenty minutes, then it eases once I'm pottering in the kitchen.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it lock, or give way under you?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It doesn't give way, and it hasn't locked.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): What are you using on it?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The gel from the chemist, diclofenac. I rub it on two or three times a day. And sometimes the tablets if it's a bad day.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which tablets? Say that again, I was typing.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen, the four hundred milligram ones. One tablet, maybe two or three times in the week.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any stomach trouble with them?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no stomach problems at all. I'm grand that way.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your weight — the last reading on here is 89 kilos. Still about that?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): God. I was twelve stone for years. I'm after putting on with the baking, the grandchildren come of a Sunday and I make the queen cakes.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): So heavier than that. Any idea what you weigh now?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I haven't a scales. A few kilos more, I'd say, but I wouldn't know exactly.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): The extra weight loads the knee, especially on stairs.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I know. Easier said than done, with the cakes.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Up on the couch and I'll have a look.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand. Mind the shoes, they're mucky from the garden.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): There's crepitus when I bend the right knee. No big effusion that I can feel. Tender on the medial joint line.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the very spot.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Flexion stops around a hundred degrees. No redness, and the foot pulses are fine.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): It won't fold back like the left one. I was worried it was the circulation — my father had the bad legs.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Vascular trouble, was it?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): He had the bypass in his seventies. Smoked like a chimney. I never smoked, thank God.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any bother in the other joints, the hips or the hands?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): The hands are grand. The left knee is a small bit achey if I walk the whole way to the shops, nothing like the right.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): How far can you walk?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I can manage the shops. It's the stairs and the night that annoy me. Oh, and I do get heartburn of an evening, especially if I've taken one of those tablets.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heartburn. You said there was no stomach trouble.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I wasn't counting that. It's a burning after the tea, up in the chest, not a pain in the belly. I take Rennies for it.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often is it, and how long has it been going on? The cursor stuck — say that again.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Most evenings lately. A couple of months, maybe. I can't put a date on when it started.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the Rennies, how do you take them?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Two tablets when it comes on. Not every night. They settle it mostly.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting, or black stools?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): No vomiting. The stools are a normal colour.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any other medicines — blood pressure tablets or the like?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the gel, the ibuprofen and the Rennies. Beaumont put me on a statin years ago and I stopped it, the legs were aching and I never went back.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which statin, what dose? The medication list won't load.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Atorvastatin. Twenty milligrams — or was it ten? I think twenty. Stopped two years ago.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll record atorvastatin 20 mg, stopped. We'll revisit that another day, not this morning.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand. Does the knee need an operation? The neighbour waited ages for her replacement.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't be talking surgery. It sounds like wear and tear, osteoarthritis of the right knee, though I've no x-ray today to confirm it.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): So is it the physio, or one of those injections?
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): We might try physiotherapy, or a steroid injection into the joint, but we won't decide that today.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): And the tablets, and the weight?

[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ease off the ibuprofen while the heartburn is about; if you take one, take it with food. Keep the diclofenac gel two or three times a day, and try to drop a couple of kilos. If the knee is no better in six weeks, come back and we'll choose between the physio and the injection.
